body.p: Dyatpashelaha, or Swan-like. There lived one man. He had a daughter, her name was Dyatpashelaha, who looked like a swan. The man loved his girl very much. If he gets the beast, first, he gives it to his daughter. Over time, he had two wives. They were sisters. But Dyatpashelaha was treated badly. When the husband went hunting, one of the wives said: "Let's kill Dyatpashelaha." And then one day there was a thunderstorm. Here is one of the wives and says: "Let's say to Dyatpashelaha that, they say, a thunderstorm is approaching, it is necessary to strengthen the tent. And we ourselves will hide in the tent. Let's say to her: Dyatpashelaha, crawl into the tent on your back, open your mouth and say: a-a. Dyatpashelaha strengthened the tent. Her two stepmothers can be heard saying: "Dyatpashelaha, crawl into the tent on your back." She slowly lay on her back and began to crawl, sticking her head under the door shutter. And the wives say: "Say: ah." Dyatpashelaha says: "Why?" Immediately, as soon as she opened her mouth and said "why," the stepmothers threw a red-hot thimble into her mouth. The thimble went down her throat. And the poor Dyatpashelaha died. Then the husband returned from hunting and said: "Atpashelaha, come here for the bird." Nobody comes. The two wives came out of the tent, they say to their husband: "Dyatpashelaha has died." The husband was surprised: "But she didn't get sick, did you?" The corpse of Dyatpashelaha was wrapped in new beautiful clothes and placed on a sled. The father harnessed the old stags, says: "Take my daughter to distant lands." The stag went, to distant lands, reached the other world, got up. A woman looks out of the tent and says: "The bride came to us and there is no need to look, she came herself." They took their wife to their son. It turns out that an old man and an old woman lived in this tent, and they had a son. Here the woman says: "Oh, our bride is silent." The old man struck the girl between the shoulder blades with his palm, then a thimble came out of her mouth and jumped out. Dyatpashelaha jumped up, grabbed the thimble and ran outside. She sat on a harnessed sled, drove the deer, drove away. And the old woman, audibly, swears at the old man, says: "What have you done, if you had not pulled out a thimble, this girl would not have gone home. She would live with us." And the stag brought Dyatpashelaha to her father. She says to her father: "When you left, your two wives did this: they put a thimble down my throat." The father took the wives by the legs and tore them in two. And they began to live as before.
